title: The Blue Line Through the Day
angle: Navigation apps make arrival easy to track, but can narrow attention to the route instead of the place being crossed.
paragraphs: A map app can announce “turn left” while the street itself offers a bakery window, a busker, and a row of trees dropping leaves into the gutter. The screen has a clean answer to the immediate question. The neighborhood has several less urgent things to say.

That focus is useful. A blue line can make an unfamiliar trip feel manageable, especially when time is short or the streets are confusing. There is no virtue in getting lost just to prove a point. But a route designed around arrival can make everything between here and there seem like blank space.

The odd trade is that a tool meant to help you move through a place can also make the place feel like an obstacle course. Attention goes to the next turn, the remaining minutes, the little dot staying on course. A side street becomes a deviation before it becomes a possibility.

Convenience need not be refused to be noticed. Sometimes the destination is the whole point; sometimes the walk has its own small details. A map can show where the path goes. It cannot decide whether the passing scene deserves a glance.
